It is one of the most remarkably properties of the human mind, that the consciousness of goiit may remain a long time dormant in it, producing no uneasiness and no sullering and yet, alier the lapse of years it will burst forth with most ten die power, and dtive the victim of it to actual despair. This has often been the case. A man who has committed sin, is like one bitten by a mad dog The momenta y pam is slight. The wound soon heals. It may keep up Iroin time to time a slight irritation, just enough to remind him

occasionally of the occurrence ; but ordinarily it is forgotten, aud lie goes on with his daily amusements and pleasures, entirely unconscious of danger. Rut though the wound is healed, the dreadful infection which it has admitted into the system, is circulating insidiously there. The poison glides harmlessly along Ins veins and arteries lor week, months, years. It does not mar his enjoyments or disturb his repose, but still the dreadful enemy, though slumbering, is there. At last, in some unexpected hour, it rises upon him in all itsstrength and overwhelms and conquers him entirely. It brings agony to his body, and indescribable horror to bis soul, and hurries him through the most furious paroxysms of madness aud despair, to inevitable death. Every person, therefore, who commits sin, takes a viper into bis bosom, a viper which may delay stinging him for many years, but it will sting him at last, unless it is removed, lie is unaware of the misery that awaits him, but it must come, notwithstanding. This is particularly the case with sins against God; and the wonder is that the sense ol guilt will remain so entirely dormant as it often does, so that no warning, no expostulation, no remonstrance will disturb the death-like repose and yet at last the volcano will ollen burst forth spontaneously, or from some apparently trilling cause, aud overwhelm the sinner in sullering.

ANECDOTE OF SIR SYDNEY SMITH. A curious circumstance connected with the services of Sir Sydney Smith, when going out to the Rrazils, as commander in chief on the South American station, it may not be amiss to mention here. On the passage to Rio Janeiro the Foudroytutf put into the island of Saint Jago (one of the Gape do Verds) tor water, and the admiral received an invitation to dine with the Governor, at his excellences mud palace on the hill- This invitation Sir Sydney accepted, and wont according to his usual mode, in great state, accompanied hv a guard of marines, and aide-de camp, and several of his officers. Just previous to sitting down to tables gentleman of grave deportment, having the appearance of an ecclesiastic, wjh dark bushy hair on his head and spectacles astride his noise, u g introduced in company with several otheis, who were stated to he prosecuting researches in botany &c\ and exploring the sins of volcanic eruptions. The interview with Sir Sydney w-as only momentary, the man of science took his seat at a distance from the admiral who, after placing himself at the board, issued some directions in an under tone to his orderly. In a few minutes, to the great astonishment and consternation of the Portuguese Governor, the guard of marines entered the dining-room, and Sir Sidney without disturbing himself, ordered two sentries to he placed at the door. He then went forward so as to get a view of the botanist and addressing him in that polite tut commanding manner which, to this celebrated

seaman, was at all times perfectly natural he said : þÿ " Monsieur Colonel, this is the fortune of war, and we have again met. I was once vour prisoner, you are now mine; finish your dinner and we will discuss other matters afterþÿwards. It was. in fact, a French officer, who find held Sir Sydney in custody in France, and was now, under the cloak of science acting as a spy having been landed fre a schooner, carrying American col. mis, that had been seen to windward of ihe island, hut, by some secret communication from the shore, made off as soon as the scheme failed. The captive was removed to the flag-ship and conveyed to Rio, where he was delivered up to the Portuguese authorities, and condemned to >he mines of San Paulo for life. þÿ Whether he was released or not subsequently I do not recollect, but I perfectly remember the story being current on the station, when I served out there under the gallant admiral. We do not propose to go into the legal hearings ol tins case at all, but merely Co refer to a tew ihings which have been said and done, by various learned doctors, touching the alleged insanity, or mental imbecility, of this woman. We believe six physicians were selected to examine her. and they visited her at various times; and merely by conversations with her, attempted to satisfy themselves as to whether she was insane or not. The testimony of the physicians was given before the Commissioner on her examination, and has already been spread beloie the public. They did not agree at all. Though these physicians were rd the fust respectability in their profession, yet, we believe, not one of them has any acquaintance w ith the science of Phrenology. This was much to he regretted ; lor we hold, thai it is not possible lor any man to have a tiue apprehension of the nature or laws of mind, without a knowledge of phrenology. From Relit Weekly Messenger, London November 4. 1844. Proceedings of the French on the Coast of Morocco. We copv the following statement f om a letter from Gibraltar : þÿ þÿ The Zaffarine Islands (IslasChafietinas) þÿ of which the three form a trianuglar group « tf Cape Aqua, on the Morocco coast, in longitude about 2 deg. 25 min. west, and winch are little more than eight leagues distant from the Spanish town and fortress of Mellila, on the main þÿland have always been in the pos sesson of Spain, and were temporarily, with the assent of that country it is presumed, occupied by the French during the late expedition against Morocco. But now that peace has been concluded, the treaties signed and the terms ratified, what further necessity is there for the occupation of this very import, ant position by the troops of Fra ace ? The great depth of water within these islands and the mainland, and the perfect protection w hich they afford on tire north and east, particularly in gales of wind, render this station unquestionably one of the finest anchorage roadsieads on the whole north coast of Africa. Whether Spain has ceded temporary or permanent occupation of them, is stiii unknown ; but considering the importance which was attached to the island of Mogador, which, as a naval station, can bear no comparison with the Zallarine Islands, it is not a little surprising that public attention has not hitherto been directed to this þÿsubject. The above named islands are situated little more than three quarters of a league from the coast of Morocco, north ol Cape Aqua, and

near Tlemcen and Ouehda. The most westerlv island of the group is composed of high land, on which grows excellent timber ; the second is less elevated ; and the long< st and most easterly is flat and low. Their position is triangular, forming a natural roadstead, with the finest anchorage ground in the Mediterranean, thus affording pet feet protection to vessels of the argest size from every wind, hut especially those of the north and east, which blow with great severity, and from which n > like shelter is to be found elsewhere on the whole coast. Their distance from Oran is about 20 leagues The possession if these islands must he of the utmost importance to the French in the event of war against Morocco, for bv means of Artesian wel s, which might be sunk, or from the tiver on the opposite mainland, where the water is abundant and of excellent quality, a fleet could be well supplied. On the lower island the different strata are so exposed, and the rniueia s composing them so suitable for building ot every description, that a tow n or fortifications could be constructed at very lit le trouble or expense. Having military possession of these islands, the French could command access at any moment to the very interior of Morocco, Mellila being only 44 leagues distant from Fez, arid the natural protection afforded hy the line of mountains (the Q.uibdanasl, which run nearly parallel with the sea and extend from Oran to the lower \tlas, would render the movement of an army a matter of easy

accomplishment i he Moots, who inhabit all this district of country to the frontier of Algeria, beiong to the tribe of Maztize, a hold and warlike people, and from their habits and occupations as contrabandists connive in a great measure to keep themselves iiidependet t of the Emperor ; so much so, that it is notorious the government in collection of tribute is almost always obliged to have recourse to an army to enforce it. From the New York Commercial Advertiser, December 7, la-it. LATER FROM MEXICO. Important þÿIntelligence. II v the arrival at the Southwest Pass of the English Innate Spartan, Hon. ("apt. Elliot, commander, which vessel sailed from Vera Crux on the 1 7th inst., we have intelligence 15 days later from Mexico. The city was rife with rumors vesterdav morning, to the effect that our Minister to Mexico, the Hon. Wilson Shannon, had demanded his passports and was on his way home, and also that a serious revolution had broken out in Mexico which had resulted in the overthrow of Santa Anna, There certainly was some foundation for this startling intelligence ; hut the new s does not turn out as important as was at fiist inputted, although still ol a momentous na tore. To a commercial house of this city we were last evening indebted for lull files ol the Uiario del Gobierno and El hiyio Diez y Nueve up to the 12th þÿinstant. We give as much of the news as we can find room for. It would appear from such ot the published correspondence as we have seen in the Dinrio that on the 31st ult.. Gov Shannon addressed a letter to the Mexican Government, protesting against the proposed invasion of Texas by Mexico, and especially against the manner in which the invasion was to he made. To this the Minister of foreign affairs replied þÿ (we have not seen his communication) denying the right of the United Slates þÿ or any other foreign government t<> interfere in the internal affairs of the republic. Gov. Shannon in answer, characterizes the Secretary's letter as being grossly offensive,

inasmuch as it charges the United States, its government and people with falsehood, trickery, intrigue and designs of I lie most dishonor;! hie character. Gov. Shannon alleges that the note of the Secretary is so gross in its character, so offensive, that he can only demand that it be at once withdrawn. The Mexican Minister replies with the utmost warmth. He treats the earlier part of Mr. Shannon's correspondence as being supercilious and offensive, justifies all that he lias himself written, proteststhat the Mexican government lias done and is doing all that it can to prevent a rupture with the United Slates, hut that atlaiis have reached such a crisis that it is necessary for his government to speak out plainly before the world. He therelore declines to withdraw the note. From the tone of this letter, it is evident enough that the Mexican Minister is of the opinion that Mr. Shannon does not speak t fie sentiments of a majority ol the people of the United Slates in relation to the Texas question. He considered too, that otir recent Presidential contest must have resulted in the election of Mr. Clay, and he speaks of that gentleman, Mr. Adams, and the United Stales Senate in terms the most dainty, while he holds Mr. Tyler's administration alone res ponsihle lor the present complication of affairs between the two countries. What elfccl the result ot Mr. Polk's election may have in Mexico, we ate unable to say.

'1 he Southern mail this afternoon may bring us something notable, judging from the following revelations, given lu a letter to the Evening Post : þÿ Washington, Dec. 14, 1844. Mr. Green, the bearer of despatches from our minister in Mexico, arrived here by yes. let day's curs, and immediately repaired to the

State Department. A cabinet council was instantly cal'ed, and their deliberations lasted far into the night. Day before yesterday, and a part of the night, Air. Calhoun spent in an earnest con ference with Air. Pakenham, the British Minister, and immediately afterward four or five different messengers were sent off from the Stale Department to several of our ministers at the different Courts in Europe, to Mexico, and to some of i lie South American Republics. The English minister also, I understand, sent oil a messenger with despatches to Great Britain. The critical condition of our relations with Alexico, and through her possibly with some of the leading powers of Europe, renders this unusual diplomatic activity a matter of deep interest and anxious speculation ; and among other on dils is one, that if Texas will, in any sufficiently authoritative manner, declare Iter wishes to become annexed to the United States, then Great Britain is to throw no obstacles in the wavt and will intimate to Mexico that it will be necessary for her to acquiesce as gracefully as she may ; that no opposition is to be expected from any other European quarter ; that a very liberal treaty of boundary will be negociated with Mexico, in which the large claims due by her to our citizens will in some satisfactory manner he arranged; and, finally, that in the general balance sheet, which is now in the progress of being made up, the Oregon boundary will also be satisfactorily adjusted. We copv the following extract of a private letter from the Morning Post : þÿ "Stettin, Dec. 4. þÿ \ II business is at a stand here. At half-past three yesterday afternoon a tire broke out in Schmidt's distillery, which quickly communicated itself to the next house, and then to their warehouses, where were lying 5000 qrs. of rapeseed ; this made such an awful blaze that it threatened to be a second Hamburg, and may yet become so. The fire has f jrned through the Hull werk to the Oder street. The wind being from south-east, every person in the Oder street moved their furniture, expecting fur certain that the whole street must burn þÿ At present the strong walls have prevented the fire spreading further that way, and if the walls stand on the other side all may stop there; but. should they fall, the whole marketplace must go. Besides which, there arc 1000 hints, of spirits lying in Schmidt's vaults, which they sav are tire-proof, but, if they do burn, the whole town must go. The worst thing is that the river is frozen over, and the engines aic so frozen that they cannot work
þÿ several men are killed. 1 saw myself three men covered by a wall that fell upon them. þÿ The mail leaves þÿ the lire continues us before."

MEETING OF THE BISHOPS. The Times publishes the following important notice from a correspondent : þÿ The Archbishop of Canterbury has announced his intention to summon a meeting of the Bench of Bishops, in consequence of the unhappy schism which at present agitates the Church of England, in order to deliberate and determine upon the rubrical observances to be enforced throughout the various dioceses of England over which his Grace has juiisdiction. It was originally intended that the meeting of the prelates should fie held at l.uinbeth Palace in the approaching Ember Week, previous to the ordinations, hot t fie melancholy death of the mother of the Bishop of London has caused the postponement of the contemplated meeting. As vet it is therefore mid termiried whether t ho assein binge of the Bench of Bishops shall take place atiout the period of the annual convocation of Si Paul's, or whether the synod shall take place at the commencement of the ensuing mouth of January. The issuing of i tie recent pastoral letter of the Bishop of Exeter tias caused fresh excitement among tfie laitv, and a new source of embarrassment to the Church; it is, therefore, not at all improbable that an early day will be determined upon by their lordships, so that the feverish controversies relative to the gown and surplice, and t lie weekly Olfertory, may lie finalU disposed of. in connection with the above subject, meetings of the rural deans of the various archdeaconries are now being assemtded, and minutes of their proceedings will tie forward-

ed to their respective bishops, in which will he explicitly stated the manner and form ol celebrating Divine Service in the dilleretil parochial churches, as well as the compliance with the rubric by the elerg\ in their deanery. It is currently reported, with some degree of authority, thai his Grace the Archbishop of ( 'nnterbuiy will, at the deliberations of the Episcopal Bench, propose a conciliatory course to be pursued relative to the observance of the rubric, so that a due regard may be paid to the sciuples of the laity relative to innovations in the Church service which may give olTenee to the congregation. In tins measure, it is also said, Ins Grace of York fully concurs.

Tub Lapi.vnorks þÿ Mr. Milford, of St. lohn's College, Cambridge, in bis very pleasing narrative of a visit made by him last year to Norway, gives the following account of his encounter with a family of Laplanders: þÿ The next morning, 27th August was rainy, and the hills were all covered with clouds; wo breakfasted at four. 011 broiled capercailzie and brandy and water, but were weather b >nii(l at liorvignou till tluee o'clock p. m, when we embarked in two small and erazv floats on Lake Eimingen. There was far more motion than I liked, the nature of our vessels being duly considered. We were, however, safely landed on some rocks, after a row of ten English miles, and then set off to walk four more, partly through woods. In our route we passed bv u sietter hut, where as I have before remarked, the peasants who pasture their cows in the neighbourhood keep their milk, cream and cheeses. We next

T V & t/ 'I X -VT2 3, crossed some barren mountains; and, at about half past seven, our guide (the Lapp) desired us not to lite at a pack of ptarmigan, which got close up to us, for fear, lie said, of distui bing the reindeer, as he every moment expected to find fiis countrymen. Soon after as we were all walking in a single file, and keeping perfect silence, he stopped suddenly ami pointing with fits finger, directed our attention to some smoke just seen issuing tluoiigli the twilight, cutting up the side of the opposite hill. The man's manper and attitude were quite dramatic, and we had I lie satisfaction ol feeling that our object was about to he attained. The Lapp now tied up Ins dog and ran off, evident!) much rejoiced at the idea of rejoining Ins wife and family, after an absence of several months. He was also anxious to inform his countrymen who we were, and what brought ns here, as lie had some fear lest they should take alarm and move oil with their herd. He soon, however, returned, and at the same time we saw a large number of reindeer driven up the valley to their quarters for the night, by a man and a boy accompanied by a dog whose occasional bark seemed to keep them under perfect control. Upon our arrival, we found the encampment consisted of two citcular tents built of poles joined together in the centre, in the form of a cone, with cloth stretched over them. The door of the larger one, in which we took up our abode, was so low and small that we had some difficulty in crawling in. The whole

scene was highly piclutesque. Each tent was occupied by a Lapp fan ilv ; every individual gave us a most kind reception and heartily shaking us by tbe hand, at once offered us a share of their tent, t fie only night's lodging they had to give We thankfully accepted their hospitality, and soon found ourselves lying on skins before a laige and cheerful fire. The inhabitants of the hut comprised three generations of Lapps ; namely, a middle aged man and Ids wde w ith four children, and an old grandmother ; to these were now added our party, consisting of four English men, their two interpreters, and two other attendants. The tent was made of coarse dark cloth, and the outside of it was covered with turf; around the inside were hung cheeses, bladders, dried gut of reindeer, guns, and various other useful articles. The chief part of the smoke- escaped through a large opening at t fie top, but enough remained painfully to affect our eyes, and to give the copper countenances of the Lapps a shade as dark as those of Indians. The second family, who occupied the smaller tent, namely, our late Lapp guide, Peter Johansen, his wife and two children, soon came to pay us a visit. 1 have already described his person. His wife and daughter had light hair and fair complexions, and were pleasing in llirir appearance, and his little hoy was an intelligent and interesting eliild, and although under ten years of age, took his turn with the men in watching the reindeer during the night ; he was dressed in his best clothes, entirely made

of skins, with a girdle round his waist and such a protuberance in front as to give him the appearance of being sttifled, and greatly to excite our laughter. He wore his knife in his case behind, and several small ornaments by his side, thus forming a complete Lilliputian l.app in full costume. We were soon presented with a large bowl of reindeer milk, which is much richer

than that of the cow, and has a delicate and aromatic flavor, with a pleasant taste, resembling the milk of the cocoa nut ; hut 1 found I could not lake much of it with impunity, as it was more like drinking cream than milk. They also boiled for usa reindeer ham, which had only been salted two days before We found it sogood that, upon taking ourdepartuie next morning, we were glad to add it to our scanty store of provisions. It has a wild flavor, and is quite equal to our park venison. The old grandmother was as shrivelled as a mummy, but the other two women were by no means ill looking. Their dress was of dark woolen cloth, with silver ornaments in front, as well as in the girdle round the waist, to which sewing implements were suspended. These ornaments were in good taste and well finished, and the buttons wete similar to those used by the peasantry in Spain. I have no doubt this smart costume was put on in compliment to us. The dress of the men consisted of leather coats and tight trousers of the same material with reindeer skin boots. All the females smoked ; and the old woman seemed more pleased with having her pipe filled with tobacco brought from England than with anything else that we gave her. Some boxes of lucifer matches whieh we presented to them were also highly prized ; they had evidently never seen them before and expressed no small astonishment at the manner in which ignition is effected. We regretted we had no fish hooks, which they inquired for ; but we gave them a glass of finkel each, which

the octogenarian appeared to relish more than any of her descendants. 1 he head of the family )John Neilson) was a grave sedate looking man ; decision of character and intelligence were marked on his fina countenance. In reply to the question I put to him through my interpreter, he said they were happy in the enjoyment of their wandering pastoral life ; that they confined themselves to the mountainous ridge which seriates Norway from Sweden, the boundary line between these countries being only two English miles from the spot where they were then encamped ; that they had been there about eight days, intended to remain a fortnight longer, and should then move onward for a change of pastuie for their reindeer. He told me, that in Summer they conduct these animals, which constitute their wealth to il.e elevated parts of the mountains, and in the Winter they descend to the level country. His herd consisted of nb< ut three hundred and it appears a family requires nearly that number for its support. 'J he great proportion of tliem were his own property, but some belonged to Peter Johansen, and ten to a middle aged single woman who lodged with them. These Lapps, although dwellers in tents all the year round, are in many respeets far from being uncivilized. They strictly observe the Sabbath, the best reader of the family officiating as priest, and going regularly through the Lutheran service Occasionally, they attend the church at the nearest village on the frontier of Sweden." þÿ

American Paper. Improvement in the Commercial Prospects of Ireland. We have been much gratified lately by noticing in some of the Irish papers statements of a verv encouraging nature respecting the prosperous condition ol sevetai blanches of

mm4 trade and commerce, and more especially of the revival of what may justly be called the staple manufacture of that country, the linen trade. In confirmation of these statements, we have much pleasure in copying into our columns the following article from the Dublin Mercantile Advertiser : þÿ " In manufacturing enterprise there is, unfortunately, so limited a ranee in this country that we have seldom to notice the fluctuations of the markets, and there are no regular reports of the state of trade, such as thus6 furnished from the English manufacturing districts. Occasionally, however, we have endeavoured to obtain the most correct information as to our staple manufacture, the linen trade, and we rejoice to be able to state that it is now in a healthy and prosperous rondi tion. We have received from a Helfast correspondent the following very grabbing report : þÿ The linen trade of Ulster is steadily progressing. For English as well as home consumption the demand is very good, and for cloth of sound and weighty fabric there is a very extensive demand from England1 The spinning trade, in late years so important a traffic, is now very brisk.' " At the different Irish ports a manifest improvement has taken place in commercial matters, and at no period tor many years have there been less complaints of distress amongst traders, shopkeepers, or farmers. This gratifying state of things is, in a great measureowing to the late excellent harvest ; and the improvement of trade in England has, no

doubt, re-acted favourably here, " The prospects for the future are, also, very encouraging. Some at least of the projected railway companies will obtain the sanction of parliament, and a considerable amount of employment will be the result . thus affording a prospect of relief to the myriads of our people who have been sunk in almost hopeless destitution. No svmptoinsof improvement could be sound or permanent which failed to reach the mass of the population. amongst whom there is so little o' remunerative employment, and with a tota' w nit of the means of obtaining even the necessaries of life We mav hope, however> from the present indications of a better state -I trade and commerce, that the poor man's industry will soon find a belter market, and that he will participate in the general improvement of the country. " \ contemporary, the Belfast Mercantile Register, gives the following verv favourable report of that district : þÿ ' Commercial prosperity still smiles on tiiis part of the country: our farmers arc comparatively well paid for their produce of the last season's bountiful harvest, and our weavers and other workmen have abundance of employment with wellpaid wages wtio can purchase good food at very moderate prices. Under these circumstances all classes are emerging from the straitened condition in which four or five seasons of agricultural scarcity and deranged commerce had involved them All classes are now great consumers, not only ol the necessaries hut of tne luxuries of life j hence the increased
demand for articles of food and clothing-'" Di li's Weekly Messenger, December 9.

Electric f't,wk', þÿ fhe following interesting extract from a letter from Mr. Finlaison, of Eoughton Hall, appears in the Polytechnic Review:--" I think you will he pleased to hear that .\lr, Uain lias succeeded

to admiration in working electric clocks by the currents of the earth. On the 28th of August, he set up a small clock in rny drawing room, the pendulum of which is in the hall and both instruments in a voltaic circuit, as follows þÿ On the N. E. side of my house, two zinc plates, each a foot square, ate sunk in a hole and suspended to a wire- This wire is passed through the house to the pendulum first and then to the clock. On the S. Eside of the house, at a distance of about 40 yards, a hole was dug four feel deep, and two sacks of common coke buried in it 5 among the coke another wire was secured, and passed 'a at the drawing room window, and joined to the former wire at the clock. The ball of the pendulum weighs 0 lb., but it was moved energetically, and has ever since continued with the selfsame energy. The time kept is to perfection, and the cost of the motive power was only 7s. tid. There are but three little wheels in the clock, and neither weights nor springs ; so there is nothing to be wound up. To another friend at Battersea, he hus given three clocks, two small ones and one a hall clock, all moved by one current, and regulated by one and the same pendulum. This is all he has completed in England, having just reached Edinburgh, where he is to establish a manufactory of these clocks, which for accuracy. cheapness, and utility, will, J believe, surpass every timepiece hitherto connived."

Long Nails in þÿChina. In a secluded hermitage at Poctoo ee, we found a man who probably had seen some eighty summers, a venerable looking priest, bis beard white as driven snow. Our attention was, however, immediately distracted from nil other portions of his person to that of his left hnnd. To use a nautical phrase, we perceived " lashed" at the back of each finger a narrow slip of bamboo, as a means ol defending the nail from any casual blow ; indeed, without this, they could not have lasted without breaking, even for a week, At oor request he carefully removed one or two of these splints. He said he had cherished these feline weapons he knew not how many years, and through Hint of great care, during the whole time without accident. It is needless to add, that this hand was totally useless to him. VVe had the curiosity to measure the longest, and found it to exceed eleven inches in length; they tapered considerably towards the point, and at the

extremities much resembled shrivelled quills. 1 heard of an old man at Amoy who possessed a nail seventeen inches in length ; but, not having seen it myself, 1 cannot vouch lor the fact ; if so, it beats my Poo too ee friend by half a foot. This elegant habit, as you will readily believe, is confined solely to those whose manners of life are entirely ftee from manual exertion ; but so common is the practice, that the very fact of not possessing what some would call these hideous talons, is here as sure a mark of man being devoid of neatness, or rather, perhaps, 1 should say dandyism, as a splay foot, a bad cut coat, or a dirty glove would be at home. þÿ Cunningham's Recollections.

A Desperate Case. þÿ The following curious circumstance is related in a letter from Toulon: þÿ Three Arabians, condemned to death, were ordered to be executed at Tenyat-el Had. On arriving at the bivouac of Cidi-Abd-el Ruder Boumedfa, the culprits placed themselves close to a lire, nod apparentlv prayed with gieat fervour. But instead of praying, they were secretly occupied in tiling their chains, which they did w ith a most extraordinary agility. They then begged front one of the gendarmes some lire to light their pipes, and whilst the gendarme was stooping to light a match, one of tliern seized him by the waist, threw him into the fire, and the whole of them escaped.

In one of these letters we find the following singular statements: þÿ " A lady of highly respectable family and station, resident for the season at Bath entered the shop of one of the most considerable drapers of that city, and purchased some trifling articles She also asked to See some pieces of expensive lace. Some were shown to her ; and, while apparently examining the quality of different pieces, she was seen by one of the assistants at another counter to abstract and secret one of the cards. She was allowed to leave the shop; was instantly followed, stopped, brought back, and the card of lace found upon her. A constable was sent for. and the lady was given into his charge. Upon being brought before the magistrate, the charge was investigated, and the proof being deemed sufficiently strong to warrant a committal, the accused was committed for trial ; the | rosecutor and the witnesses were hound over to appear and give evidence at the next assizes. Various efforts were made to induce the siiopkeepet to forego the prosecution j but he resisted every inducement. He had prosecuted others whose poverty was the proirq ter of their offences ; and he Would not screen one who had no such temptation to dishonesty.

The assizes approached ; and public excitement ran high at the prospect of the lady thief being arraigned at the bar of a criminal tribunal. Some time fiefoie the assizes a lady of apparently high respectability entcicd the shop of the prosecu o , and made several trifling purchases. Among other articles she bought some lace. The trial of the lady who stood committed on the charge of stealing a card of lace from the same shop, came on at the assizes, and the evidence in support of the charge was adduced. The lady in whose muff the card of lace was so mvsteriously found Was, of course, produced as a witness on behalf of the accused ladv. The Blind Husband and the Exemflarv Wife. þÿ The Paris correspondent of the Intelligencer in a recent letter, beauiifully chronicles a painful event as follows; " The first historian of France þÿ still longer sightless þÿ and yet Comparatively young, A ngostin Thierry, lost, in the first week of the month, his accomplished and most exemplary wife. She produced books of her own, successful in every respect, but renounced authorship for undivided conjugal devotion. In a beautiful record of her demise, ascribed to her husband's pen, it is truly said ; 'Asa solace for his misfortune, Providence gave him, in Madame Thierry, the hand that held his pen, the heart on which he leaned, and the eves which saw him ' He became her sole thought, and his name was the last sound from her lips." The above extract shows that the inrxhaustible wealth of a pure affection, is far beyond the treasures of intellect, or the value of actual riches. The " world of the affections" is rightly the realm of woman, and the sweet duty ot her love is far beyond the light of her intellect, as Long-fellow has written, " The intellect is finite; but the affections Are injiuit and cannot fie exhausted." The extract from Mr. Walsh's letter above given, conveys a noble eulogy upon woman þÿ and the editor of the United States (Phil ) Gazette, who never petmitsa beautiful thought, a noble action, or an elevated sentiment 10 escape him Unnoticed, comments upon the passage as follows ; How rare, how very rare þÿ not the virtues,

but the eulogy I Such qualities as Thierry lauds in his departed wife, are common to the sex. The position of the recipient of these blessings was unusual ; and that gave extraordinary operation to the characteristics of her from whom these blessings flowed. Thierry, 11 would seem, was a man of sufficient sense to treat a woman as his equal, not his counterpart ; as Ins equal, to comprehend and acknowledge her powers to perform, and to confess ihe greater power of forbearance. One half of the deficiencies of what man complains of in man, woman, and child, are the results of want of confidence. The field is left to weeds, because no one will entrust to its bosom the seeds of profitable vegetation. The first historian of France received from Providence what might have been a thoughtless at least, an unaflectionate woman. Hia heart was rightly touched; his necessities (perhaps) bade him lean upon her heart; his blindness asked the aid of her eyes, lie leaned, and was sustained, he confided and her vision supplied his wants; and ber love for her husband was repaid and improved by gratitude. tor having allowed her the means ol exhibiting her capabilities as a woman and a þÿwife and hence her parting weird, the lost on earth, was her husband's name. Wives þÿ women in general þÿ owe to Af. Thierry, constant thanks lor his magnanimit V that allowed ot a full (Jispjny of female excellence. And they should bless the memory of Madame T hierry, who so beautifully and attractively illusiialtd the character ol Woman

One of the chief objections which was urged against it, was found to consist in the tact that the question of annexation had not been submitted to ttie ordeal of public opinion in the United States. However untenable such an objection was esteemed to be, in view ol the unquestionable power of the Executive to negociuie the treaty, and the great and lasting interests involved in t tie question, I felt it to be my duly to submit t tie whole subject to Congress as the best expounders of popular sentiment. No cfeliaitive action having been taken on the subject Ey Congress, the question referred itself directly to the decision of the States and the people. The great popular election which has just terminated, afforded the best opportunity of ascertaining the will of the States and people upon it. Bending that issue, it became the imperative duty of the Executive to inform Mexico that the question of annexation was still before the American people, and that,

until their decision was pronounced, any serious invasion oi Texas would be regarded as an attempt to forestall their judgment, and could not be looked upon with indifference. I am most happy to inform you that no such invasion has taken place, and 1 trust that, whaiever your action may be u on it, Mexico will see the importance of deciding the niattei by a resort to peaceful expedients, in preference to those of arms. The decision of the people and the States, on this great and interesting subject has been decisively manifested. The question of annexation has been presented nakedly to their considetation. By the treaty itself, all collateral and incidental issues, which were calculated to divide and distract the public councils, were carefully avoided. These were left to the wisdom of the future to determine. It presented, I repeat, the isolated question of annexation ; and in that form it has been submitted to the ordeal of public sentiment. A controlling majority of tlte people, and a large majority of the states, have declared in favor of immediate annexation Instructions have thus come up to both branches of Congress, from their respective constituents, in terms the most emphatic. It is the will of both the people and the States, that Texas shall be annexed to the Union promtly and immediately. It may he hoped that, in carrying into execution the public will, thus declared all collateral issues may be avoided. Future Legislatures can best decide as to the number

of States which should be formed out of 'he territory, when the time has arrived for deciding that question. So with all others. By the treaty lire United States assumed the payment of the debts of Texas to an amount not exceeding 10.000,000 to be paid, w ith the exception of a sum falling short ol $41)0.- 000, exclusively out of the proceeds of the sales of her public lands. We could not, with honor, take the lands, without assuming the full payment of all incumbrances upon them.

Nothing has occurred since your last session to induce a doubt that the dispositions of Texas remain unaltered. No intimation of an altered determination, on the part of her Government and þÿi eople, lias been furnished to i Ire Executive. She still desires to throw herself under the protection of our laws, and to partake of the blessings of our federative system ; while every American-intertst would seem to require it. The extension of our coastwise and foreign trade, to an amount almost incalculable-the enlargement of the market for our þÿmanufactures a constantly growing market for our agricultural produclions þÿ safety to our frontiers, and additional strength and stability to the Union þÿ these arc the results which would rapidly develope themselves, upon the consummation of the measure of annexation. In such event, 1 will not doubt bat that Mexico would find her true interest to consist in meeting the advances ol this Government in a spirit ot amity. Nor do l appreitend any serious complaint from any other quarter ; no suliicient ground exists for such complaint. We should inter, fere in no respect with the rights of any other nation. There cannot be gathered from the act, any design on our part to do so wiih their possessions on this Continent. We have interposed no impediments in the way of such acquisitions of territory, large and extensive as many of them are, as the loading powers of 1 Europe have made, from tune to time, in every

part of the world. We seek no conquest made bv war. No intrigue will have been resorted lo, or acts of diplomacy essayed, to accomplish the annexation ol Texas. Free, and independent herself, she asks to be received into our Union. It is a question for our own decision, whether site shall be received or not, The two Governments having already agreed, ihrough their respective organs, on the terms of annexation, I would recommend their adoption by Congress in the form of a joint resolution, or act, to be perfected and made binding on the two countries, when adopted in like inanuer by the Government of Texas. In order that the subject may he fully presented in all its bearings, the correspondence which has taken place, in reference to it, since the adjournment of Congress, between the United States, Texas and Mexico, is herewith transmitted. The amendments proposed by the Senate to the Convention concluded between the United States and Mexico on the 20ih of November, 1843, have been transmitted through our Minister, for the concurrence ol the Mexican Government; but, although urged thereto, no action has yet been had on the subject ; nor has any answer been given which would authorize a favorable conclusion in the future. iiave ted to a correspondence of considerable length between the Minister for Foreign Relations and our Representative at Mexico, but without any satisfactory result. It remains for Congress to make the necessary appropriation to carry the arrangement into effect, wiiicii I respectfully recommend. The greatly improved condition of the Treasury, atldrds a subject for general congratulation. The paralysis which had fallen on trade and commerce, and which subjected tiie Government to the necessity of resorting to loans, and the issue of Treasury notes, to a large amount, has passed awav. and after

the payment of Upwaids of $7 000(190, on account of the interest, and in redemption of more than 5, 000,000 of the public debt, which falls due on the 1st of Jarmarv next, and sennit! apa t upwards of $'2,0t>0,000 for the payment of outstanding Treasury notes,

In a new country like that of the U. States, where so many inducements are held out for speculation, the depositories of the surplus revenue, consisting of Banks of any description, w hen it reaches any considerable amount, require the closest vigilance on the part of the Goveminent. All banking institutions, under whatever denomination they may pass, are governed by an almost exclusive regard to the interest of the stockholders. That inter-

est consists in the augmentation of profits, in tiie form of dividends, and a large surplus revenue entrusted to their custody is but too apt to lend to excessive loans and to extravagantly large issues of paper. As a necessary consequence, prices are nominally ineieased and the speculative mania everywhete seizes upon the public mind. A fictitious state of prosperity for a season exists ; and in the language of the day, money becomes plenty.

Contracts are entered into by individuals, resting on this unsubstantial state <4 things, but the delusion speedily passes away and tiie country is overrun by an indebtedness so weighty as to overwhelm many, and to visit every deparlmet t of industry with great and ruinous embarrassment. The greatest vigi lance becomes necessary on the part of Government to guard against this slate of tilings. The Government, 'through its reve. lie has. at all times, an important part lo perform in connexion with ti e currency ; and it greatly depends upon its vigilance and care, whether the country lie involved in embarrassments similar to those which it has had recently to encounter ; or, aided by the action of tiie Treasury shall be preserved in a sound and healthy condition. tutional authority ; and a reckless and wasteful extravagance but too certainly follows. Composed as is tiie Union of separate at d independent Slates a patriotic legislatuie will not tail in consulting the interests of the parts, to adopt such course as will tie best calculated to advance the hat morn of the whole, ai d thus ensure that permanency m the police of the government without which all etloits to advance the public prosperity are vain and

( Concluded ) To the Senate and House of Representatives, of the United States. 1 refer you to the report of the Secretarv of War, for an exhibition of the condition of the army ; ami recommend to you, as well worthy your best consideration, many of the suggestions it contains. The Secretary in no degree exaggerates the great importance, of pressing forward, without delay, in the work ot erecting and finishing the fortifications, to which he particularly alludes. Much has been done towards placing our cities and roadsteads in a state of security against the hazards of hostile attack, w ithin the last four years: but considering the new elements which have been, of late years, emploxed m the propelling of ships, and the formidable implements of destruction which have been brought into service, we cannot he too active or vigilant in preparing and perfecting the means of defence. 1 refer you, also, to his report for a full statement of the condition of the Indian tribes within our jurisdiction. The Executive lias abated no eflort in carrying into eliect the well established policy of the Government, which contemplates a renin, val of all the tribes residing within ihe limits of the several States, beyond those limits; ani it is now enabled to congratulate the country at the prospect of an early consummation of this object Many of the tribes have already made great progress iri the arts >! civilized life ; and through the operation of the schools established among them, aided hv

:he efforts of the pious men of various reli gious denominations þÿ who devote thcmelves to the task of their improvement þÿ we mav fondly hope that, the remains of the formica ble trifies which were once the masieis of this country will, in their transition from the savage state, to a condition of relioement and cultivation, add another bright trophy to adorn the labors of a weil altogether philanthropy. The accompanying report of the Secretary of the Navy will explain to you the situation of that branch of the service. The present organization of the Department, imparls to its operations great deficiency ; but I concur futt\c7irtheþÿ propriety of a division of the Bureau of Construction. Equipment and He pa its, into two bureaus. The subjects, as now arranged, are incongruous, and requite to a certain extent, information and qualifications already dissimilar. The operations of the squadron on the oast of Africa have been conducted with all due attention to the object which led to its organization; and I am happy to say that the officers and crews have enjoyed the best possible health under the system adopted by the officer in command. It is believed the United States is the only nation which has, by its laws, subjected to the punishment of death, as pirates, those who may he engaged io the slave trade. A similar enactment on the part of other nations would not fail to he attended by beneficial results. In consequence of the difficulties which have existed in the wav of securing titles for

the necessary grounds, operations have not yet been commenced towards the establishment of the Navy Yard at Memphis. !So soon as the title is perfected, no fuither delav wiii tie permitted to mterveue. It is well

<Q 'Si t) 2 'J& A T 2 3, worthy of your consideration, whether Congress should not direct the establishment of a rope walk, in connection with the contemplated Navy Yard, as a measure not only of economy, hut as highly useful and necessary. The only establishment of the sort now con nected with the service is located at Boston ; and tlie advantages of a similar establishment convenient to the hemp growing region, must he apparent to all. The report ol the Secretary presents other matters to your consideration, of an important character tu connection with the service. In referring you to the accompanying repoit ol the Postmaster General, it allot ds me continued cause of gratification to he able to advert to the 'act, that the allairs of the Depai iment, lor the last four years, have been so conducted as, from its unaided resources to meet its large expenditures. On my coming into office a debt of nearly 500,000 existed against the Department, which Congicss iiischaiged by an appropriation from me l ieasuiy. The Department, on the 4th ol March next, will he found, under the management of the present efficient head, tree ol debt or embarrassment, which could only have been done by the observance and practice ofthe greatest vigilance anu economy. The laws have contemplated, throughout, that the Department should be self sustained ; but u may become neeessary, with the wisest regard to public interests, to introduce amendments and altei aliens in the system. There is a stiung desire manifested in many

quarters, so to alter the tariff of letter postage us to reduce the amount of tax at present imposed. Should such a measuie be carried into effect to the lull extent desired, it cannot well tie doubled hut that for the first years of its operation, a diminished revenue would be collected, the supply of which would necessarily constitute a charge upon the Treasury. Whether such a result would be desirable it will be for Congress, in its wisdom to dele: mine. It may in general he asserted, that radical alterations in any system should rather be brought about gradually, than by sudden changes ; and by pursuing this prudent policy in the teduction of letter postage, the Department might still sustain itself through the revenue which will accrue by the increase ol letters. The state and condition of the public Treasury has, heretofore, been such as to have precluded the recommendation of any mateiial change þÿ '1'he difficulties upon this head have however, ceased, and a large discretion is now left to the Government. 1 cannot loo strongly urge the policy of authorizing the establishment of a line of steamships regularly to ply between this country and foreign ports, and upon our own waters, for the transportation of the mail. 'The example of the Biitish Government is wed w orthy of imitation in this respect. The belief is strongly entertained that the emoluments arising from the transportation of mail matter to foreign countries, would operate of itself as an inducement to cause individual

euterprize to undertake that branch of the task ; and the remuneration of the Government would consist in the addition readily made to our steam navy in case of emergency by tire ships so employed. Should this suggestion meet your approval, the propriety of placing such ships under the command of experienced officers of the navy will not escape your observation- The application of steam to the purpose of naval warfare.

cogently recommends an extensive steam marine as important in estimating the def trices ol the country þÿ Fortunately, this may be attained by us to a great extent without incurring any large amount of expenditure. Steam vessels to be engaged in the transportation ol the mails on our principal water courses, lakes, and parts of our coast, could also he so constructed as to be efficient as war vessels when needed ; and would of themselves constitute a lorirtidahle force in order to repel attacks from abroad. We cannot be blind to the fact, that other nations have already added large numbers of steam ships to their naval armaments, aud that this new and powerful agent is destined to revolutionize the condition of the world It becomes the United States therefore, looking to their security, to adopt a similar policy ; and the plan suggested will enable them to do so at a small comparative cost. 1 take the greatest pleasure in bearing tes timonv to the zeal and untiring industry which has characterized the conduct of the members of the Executive Cabinet. Each in his appropriate sphere has rendered me the most efficient aid in carrying on the Government, and it will not, 1 trust, appear out of place for me to hear this public testimony. þÿ The cardinal objects which should ever be held in view by those entrusted with the administration ot public affairs, are rigidly, and without lavor or affection, so to interpret the national will, expressed m the laws, as, that injustice should he done to þÿnone justice to

all. This has been the rule upon which they have acted; and thus it is believed that lew cases, if any, exist, wherein our fellow citizens, who from time to time have been drawn to the Seat of Government lor the settlement of their transactions with the Goverrmrnt. have goneuway dissatisfied. Where the testimony has been perfected, and was esteemed satisfactory, tiieir ciaims have been promptlr audited ; and this in the at sence of all favoritism or partiality. 'ihe Government which is not just to its ow n people, can neither claim their alleclion, nor the respect of the world. At the same time the closest attention has been paid to those matters which relate more immediately to the great concerns of the country. Order and efii< iency in each bianrh of the public service, have prevailed, accompanied by a system of the most rigid responsibility on the pari of the receiving and disbursing agents. The fact, in illustration of the truth of this remark deserves to be noticed, that the revenues ol the Government, amounting in the last four years, to upwards of 8180,000.000, have been collected and disbursed, through the numerous Governmental agents, without the loss, by default, of any amount worthy of serious commentary. The appropriations made by Congress for the improvement of the rivers of the West, and of the harbors on the lakes are in a course of judicious expenditure under suitable agents; and are destined, it is to be hoped, to realize all the beneliis designed to be ac-

complished by Congress. 1 cannot, however, sufficiently impress upon Congress, the great importance of withholding appropriations Irotn improvements which are not ascertained by previous examination and survey, to be necessary for the shelter and protection of trade from the dangers of storms and tempests. Without this precaution, the expenditures are hut loo apt to ensure to the benefit of indivj. duals; without reference to the only consideration which can render them constitutional þÿ the public interests aud the general good. 1 cannot too earnestly urge upon you the interests of this District, over which, by the Constitution, Congress has exclusive jurtsdic tion. It would tie deeply to be regretted should there be. at any time, ground to complain of neglect on the part of a community which, detached as it is from the paternal care of the States of Virginia and Maryland, can only expect aid from Congress, as its local legislature. Amongst the subjects winch claim your attention, is the prompt organization of »n asylum lor the insane, who mav he

found, from time lo time, sojourning within the District. Such course is also demanded by considerations which apply to branches of the public service, For the necessities in this behalf, I invite your particular attention to the report of the Secretary of the Navy. I have thus, gentlemen of the two Houses of Congress, presented you a true and faithful picture of the condition of public allairs, both foreign and domestic. The wants of the public service are made known to you ; and matters of no ordinary importance are urged upon your consideration. Shall 1 not be permitted to congratulate you on the happy auspices under which you have assembled, ar.d at the important change in the condition of things which has occurred in the last time years ? During that period questions with foreign powers, of vital importance to the peace oi our country, have been settled and adjusted. A desolating and wasting war will) savage tribes, has been brought to a close. The internal tranquillity of the country, threatened by agitating questions, has been preserved. The credit ol the Government, which had experienced a temporary embarrassment, has been thoroughly restored. Its collets, which, for a season, were empty, have been replenished. A currency, nearly uniform in its value, has taken the place of one depreciated and almost worthless. Commerce and manufactures, which had suffered in common with every other interest, have once more revived ; and the whole country exhibits an aspect of prosperity and happi-

ness. Trade and barter, no longer governed by a wild and speculative mania, rest upon a solid and substantial tooting ; and the rapid growth of our cities, in every direction, bespeakes most strongly the lavorable circumstances by which we are surrounded My happiness, in the retirement which shortly awaits me, is the ardent hope which 1 experience, that this state of prosperity is neither deceptive nor destined to be short lived, and that measures wtiich have not yet received its sanction, but which i cannot hut regard as closely connected with the honor, the glory, and still more enlarged prosperity of the country, are destined, tit an early day, to receive the approval ol Congress. Under these circumstances, and with these anticipations, I shall most gladly lenve to others, more able than mvselt, the noble and pleasing task of susiaming the public prosperity. 1 shall carry with me into retirement the gratifying reflection that, as my sole objeet throughout has been to advance the public good, 1 may not entirely have failed in accomplishing it 5 and this gratification is heightened in no small degree hy the fact that when, under a deep and abiding sense of duty. 1 have found myself constiaiued to resort to the qualified Veto, it has neither been followed hy disapproval on the part of the people, nor weakened in any degree their attachment to that great conservative feature of our Government. THE SABBA TH AND RICH DINNERS. To the llditor of the A. I'. Sun: þÿ I hope you will permit me to sav a word in your paper in relation to the Sabbath I am employed in a very excellent family, where the Sabbath is greatly respected and all the house go to church. But, sir, I seldom get to church, as the unusually rich dinners served up on that day require extra time and labor. No one doubts that we poor servants have souls ; we love our churches ; we can feel happy as the greatest in the land under the ministrations of Heaven's Ambassadors, and why then exclude us from church for the mere gratification of the animal appetites of those who weep over the unevungelized heathen ? I think all Christians might profit by reflection upon this matter, and even those who are not Christians would do well to think of it þÿ The remedy of cold dinners will not bring with it any great self denial to the members of families. Lot us cook the Sunday dinner on Saturdav. A cup of hot coffee or tea with a piece of cold meat, might make a very good dinner for the Sabbath, and very many families follow the practice. By this meat s we might get to church, and be saved from the miseries of that ignorance of sacred things, which is now wrapped around too many of us poor servants, like a winding sluet for eternity. Pardon this intrusion upon your time and attention, Mr. Editor, and accept the assurances of sincere respect entertained for you by a poor. Servant Girl. The Drunkard's Will. þÿ 1 leave to So-

ciety, a ruined character, a wretched example. and a memory that will soon rot. I leave to my parents, during the rest of (heir lives, as much sorrow as humanity in a decrepit and feeble state, can sustain. I leave to my brothers and sisters, as much mortification and injury, as I could conveniently bring upon them. I leave to mv wife a broken heart, a life of wretchedness and shame to weep over me, and premature death. I give and bequeath to each of my children, poverty, ignorance, a low character, and the remembrance that their father was a dinnkard and n monster. Elder G. F. A. Sag Harbor, April 20th 1844.
